c.tagline: Beirut, the resilient Mediterranean capital of ruins, nightlife, and grit.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; agree on a fare in USD or LBP before the ride, or use Uber/Bolt for transparent pricing.

emergency.note: Lebanese Red Cross (140) handles most ambulance calls; response times can vary outside central Beirut.

avoid.reason: Avoid the southern suburbs (Dahieh), Palestinian refugee camps, and areas near the southern border with Israel due to ongoing security and conflict risks.
Political demonstrations downtown can turn volatile quickly and should be given a wide berth, and petty theft has risen with the economic crisis — keep valuables discreet.

hood_desc: Grand, colonnaded reconstructed core with Roman ruins, mosques, the Beirut Souks and Parliament square; upscale, quiet at night, best for luxury travelers and history buffs.
Beirut's bohemian, walkable university district with cafes, bookshops, cheap eats and nightlife; suits students, budget travelers and solo visitors who want street life.

Steep, nightlife-heavy strip of restored Ottoman/French buildings packed with bars, restaurants and galleries, spilling into industrial-chic Mar Mikhael next door; suits younger travelers wanting nightlife.
Genteel, tree-lined hillside district of Belle Epoque mansions, embassies, art galleries (Sursock Museum) and upscale dining; suits travelers wanting a quieter, elegant base.
Seafront promenade (Corniche) beside Pigeon Rocks with sea-view hotels, joggers and cafes; suits travelers who want a resort-like waterfront stay close to downtown.

water.note: Water supply is unreliable and often contaminated; use bottled water for drinking and brushing teeth.

sys.n: OMT (Ministry of Transport) public bus network

transit.pay: Pay the driver or conductor in cash (USD or LBP) directly onboard; there is no rechargeable transit card. Fares are informal and negotiated by route length.
transit.hours: Roughly 6am-8pm for most routes; very limited or no service overnight, when taxis/rideshare are used instead.
transit.note: Beirut has no metro or tram; public buses and shared "service" taxis (fixed-route shared cabs) are the main low-cost options, though most visitors rely on taxis or rideshare apps.

transit.m: OMT bus route 5 to Cola/Downtown (~40-50 min)
Shared service taxi to city center (~20-30 min)

tip.r: 10% is appreciated in restaurants (check if service charge already added); round up for taxis.

food.name: Manoushe
food.desc: Breakfast flatbread from the neighbourhood furn, spread with zaatar and olive oil or melted akkawi cheese and folded on the spot.

places.name: Ichkhanian Bakery
places.note: Armenian-Lebanese bakery running since 1946; zaatar manoushe and lahm baajin.

places.name: Barbar
places.note: Round-the-clock Hamra institution; manoushe from the oven at almost any hour.

places.name: Zaatar w Zeit
places.note: Beirut-born chain that took the manoushe late-night; reliable and open very late.

food.name: Kibbeh nayeh
food.desc: Raw lamb or beef pounded with fine bulgur, mint and onion, eaten with olive oil and raw onion; a Sunday-table centrepiece.

places.name: Abu Naim
places.note: No-frills traditional house locals go to for nayeh and old-school offal mezze.

places.name: Em Sherif Cafe
places.note: Polished all-day version of the Em Sherif kitchen; beautifully plated nayeh.

places.name: Al Falamanki
places.note: Garden house doing full mezze spreads, backgammon and arak with the nayeh.

food.name: Shawarma
food.desc: Marinated beef or chicken carved off the vertical spit into thin bread with pickles, tomato and garlic toum or tarator.

places.name: Joseph Shawarma
places.note: Cult beef shawarma counter; queues on the pavement well past midnight.

places.name: Barbar
places.note: Sprawling 24-hour complex; the default late-night shawarma stop in west Beirut.

places.name: Malak el Tawouk
places.note: Famous for garlicky chicken tawouk sandwiches, open extremely late.

food.name: Lebanese mezze
food.desc: The shared table: tabbouleh heavy on parsley, hummus, fattoush, moutabal and warm bread, ordered in waves rather than courses.

places.name: Tawlet Souk el Tayeb
places.note: Rotating farmers' kitchen where a different village cook heads the buffet daily.

places.name: Al Falamanki
places.note: Every mezze you can name plus grills and oven pies in an old villa garden.

places.name: Liza
places.note: Restored 1920s palace serving refined Lebanese mezze under painted ceilings.

food.name: Lahm bi ajin
food.desc: Thin open-faced pies of minced lamb with tomato, pine nuts and pomegranate molasses, baked crisp in a wood oven.

places.name: Ichkhanian Bakery
places.note: Armenian-style lahm baajin with a sharp pomegranate tang; the benchmark version.

places.name: Onno Bourj Hammoud
places.note: Armenian quarter kitchen known for soujouk, mante and meat pies.

places.name: Furn stalls of Bourj Hammoud
places.note: Armenian bakery lanes sell them by the tray, hot from mid-morning.

food.name: Knafeh bi jibn
food.desc: Melted sweet cheese under semolina or shredded pastry, drenched in orange-blossom syrup and eaten in a sesame kaak bun for breakfast.

places.name: Amal Bohsali
places.note: Beirut sweets house dating to 1878; classic cheese knafeh and baklava.

places.name: Abdul Rahman Hallab and Sons 1881
places.note: Tripoli dynasty's Beirut outposts; go early while the knafeh trays are hot.

places.name: Al Baba Sweets
places.note: Long-standing Hamra patisserie; knafeh in a kaak bun to eat on the street.

food.name: Arak
food.desc: Grape spirit distilled with aniseed, poured over ice until it clouds white; the standard partner to a Lebanese mezze table.

places.name: Al Falamanki
places.note: Garden tables built for slow arak-and-mezze afternoons with narghile.

places.name: Tawlet Souk el Tayeb
places.note: Pours small-producer village araks alongside the farmers' menu.

places.name: Mayrig
places.note: Armenian-Lebanese kitchen with a good arak list and a leafy terrace.

food.name: Jallab
food.desc: Chilled date and grape molasses syrup with rose water, topped with pine nuts and raisins; Beirut's summer cooler.

places.name: Al Falamanki
places.note: Proper pine-nut-loaded jallab served in tall glasses under the trees.

places.name: Hamra Street juice stalls
places.note: Pavement juice bars mix jallab and fresh cocktails de fruits all evening.

places.name: Amal Bohsali
places.note: Sweets house also does traditional drinks to go with the pastries.

landmarks: Pigeon Rocks (Raouche)
These twin limestone sea arches jutting from the Mediterranean are Beirut's most iconic natural landmark, especially stunning at sunset.
Mohammad Al-Amin Mosque
Beirut's largest mosque, with its striking blue domes and four minarets, anchors downtown's skyline and symbolizes the city's postwar revival.
National Museum of Beirut
Lebanon's premier archaeological museum houses treasures spanning millennia, from Phoenician sarcophagi to Roman mosaics, in a grand Egyptian-revival building.
Beirut Corniche
This palm-lined seafront promenade is where locals stroll, fish, and jog while taking in unbroken Mediterranean views along the coastline.
Martyrs' Square
A historic public square and symbol of Lebanese resilience, marked by the bullet-scarred Martyrs' Monument commemorating the nation's independence struggle.
Place de l'Étoile (Nejmeh Square)
This elegant clock-tower square in downtown Beirut, ringed by French mandate-era architecture and cafes, is the city's ceremonial heart.
Roman Baths of Beirut
Excavated ruins of a 2nd-century Roman bathhouse sit incongruously amid downtown skyscrapers, offering a glimpse into the city's ancient past.
Beirut Souks
A modern reimagining of the city's historic marketplace, this open-air shopping district blends archaeological remnants with contemporary boutiques and restaurants.
Sursock Museum
Housed in a restored Ottoman-era villa in the Achrafieh district, this museum showcases modern Lebanese art within a striking stained-glass facade.
Saint George Maronite Cathedral
Standing beside the Al-Amin Mosque, this Neoclassical cathedral exemplifies Beirut's interfaith coexistence and features a fascinating archaeological crypt museum below.

train.note: Lebanon has no working railway - the network has been defunct since the civil war. Travel overland by bus/shared taxi, or by sea/air.

intl.to: Damascus (Syria) - 2-3 hr via the Masnaa border
intl.op: shared taxis and vans from Charles Helou station — pay on boarding, no online booking

bus.note: No branded international coach with online booking. Shared taxis and vans to Damascus, Syria (~2-3h) depart from the Charles Helou station in central Beirut and pay-on-boarding; check the current Lebanon-Syria border and security situation before travelling.

ferry.note: The Jounieh-Larnaca passenger ferry launched in June 2026, the first Lebanon-Cyprus link in about two decades. It sails from Jounieh port, roughly 20 km north of Beirut, and crosses in under 4 hours (several departures a week). Book on the operator's site and bring your passport.
